title: Getting started
description: Get up and running with the Keplar API in minutes.

title: Quickstart
summary: Make your first Keplar API call in under five minutes.

children.text: Keplar resolves place names, coordinates, and boundaries through a single REST API. This quickstart takes you from zero to a first response.
Requests without an API key are rate limited to 10 per minute. Sign up for a free key to raise the limit.

title: Installation
summary: Install the Keplar SDK for Node.js, Deno, or the browser.

children.text: The SDK ships as an ES module with TypeScript types included. It runs in Node.js 20+, Deno, and modern browsers.
The browser build proxies requests through your own backend by default. Never expose an API key in client-side code.

title: Authentication
summary: Create API keys and authenticate requests to the Keplar API.

children.text: Every request carries a bearer token. Keys are scoped per environment, and you can rotate them without downtime by keeping two active keys during the switch.
Rotate keys from the dashboard under Settings, then API keys. Old keys keep working for 24 hours after rotation.

title: Guides
description: Task-oriented guides for common Keplar workflows.

title: Geocoding addresses
summary: Convert street addresses to coordinates, with batching and ambiguity handling.

children.text: Geocoding turns an address string into coordinates and a confidence score. The interesting problems are ambiguity and volume.

An input like 'Springfield' matches dozens of places. The API returns candidates ordered by confidence, and you decide how to disambiguate: bias by a bounding box, a country code, or the requesting user's location.
A confidence below 0.8 usually means the input is ambiguous. Surface the candidates instead of picking the first one.

title: Working with boundaries
summary: Fetch administrative boundaries as GeoJSON and test points against them.

children.text: Boundaries are polygons for administrative areas: countries, regions, municipalities, postal zones. Keplar serves them as GeoJSON with simplification levels tuned for rendering or for point-in-polygon tests.
Use the 'exact' simplification level for point-in-polygon tests and 'render' for maps. Exact polygons for a country can run to several megabytes.

title: Endpoints
summary: Every Keplar REST endpoint with parameters and response shapes.

children.text: The API is versioned in the path. The current version is v1, and breaking changes ship as v2 with at least a year of overlap.

title: Error codes
summary: What each error code means and how to recover from it.

children.text: Errors return a machine-readable code, a human-readable message, and a documentation link. Retry semantics are explicit: 429 and 503 responses carry a Retry-After header, and everything else is not retryable.
Do not retry 4xx responses other than 429. The request will fail again, and repeated failures count against your rate limit.
